entries.clue: Second downgrade is reasonable (8)

blocks.note: a mo = a second, a moment
to derate is to lower the rating of

annotation.surface: Someone argues that a second, milder downgrade is a fair outcome.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like an ordinal ('a second downgrade'), but it is the noun: a moment, MO.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a moderate price or request stays within sensible limits, which is what reasonable means.

entries.clue: Stone mason turns up checking the last word (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the letters from the bottom
the words hold the answer in check, containing it

annotation.surface: A stonemason carves the final word of an inscription on a headstone.
annotation.walkthrough: The mason and the stone suggest a gravestone inscription, which makes AMEN feel at home; the letters sit across the two words, backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Amen closes a prayer, so it is literally the last word said.

entries.clue: Fat reserves not specified at the end of the day (6)

indicators.note: to reserve is to hold something back, so SUET holds the letters inside

blocks.note: n.s. is the abbreviation for 'not specified'

annotation.surface: A diet note warns that unspecified amounts of fat pile up by evening.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reserves' reads as a noun (fat reserves in the body), but it is a verb: SUET holds NS.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: sunset marks the close of daylight, the moment the sun drops below the horizon.

entries.clue: In Yorkshire The Clangers causes nightmares (7)

annotation.surface: The gentle children's TV show The Clangers is said to give Yorkshire children bad dreams.
annotation.walkthrough: The Clangers is an old British children's TV show about knitted space creatures, so the italics make it look like a title; split off 'The' and the rest is plain blunders.
annotation.definitionFit: Terrors, like nightmares, are frightening experiences.

entries.clue: Say nothing! Husband is always primarily going on about himself (8)

definitions.note: the definition describes the behaviour; the answer names the obsession behind it

indicators.note: primarily = first of all, so take the first letters

blocks.note: first letters of is and always

annotation.surface: A wife wishes her husband would stop forever talking about himself.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say nothing!' reads as a plea for silence, but it splits into EG and O.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who is always going on about himself shows egomania, an obsessive self-regard.

entries.clue: Cracking lad married flighty type (3,7)

indicators.note: cracking breaks the letters up for rearrangement

annotation.surface: A fine young man has wed someone fickle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' reads as praise for the lad, but it is the instruction; 'flighty' is the usual word for a flirt and here means literally able to fly.
annotation.definitionFit: The red admiral is a common butterfly, a creature that takes flight.

entries.clue: Blessings received following this violent outburst? (6)

definitions.text: Blessings received following this violent outburst?

blocks.note: the surface reads as forgiveness after a row; the setter means the 'Bless you!' people say afterwards
not a burst of temper but a sudden explosive rush of air through the nose

annotation.surface: Someone is forgiven with blessings after a furious tirade.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'violent outburst' suggests temper, but it is a nasal one; people say 'Bless you' after a sneeze.
annotation.definitionFit: A sneeze is a sudden explosive expulsion of air, followed by 'Bless you'.

entries.clue: One often sleeping unleashed extremely masculine odours (8)

indicators.note: set loose, the letters run free into a new order
take the extreme letters, the first and last

annotation.surface: A sleeper gives off strong manly smells.
annotation.walkthrough: The dormouse is famous for hibernating, and the Dormouse at the Mad Hatter's tea party keeps nodding off.
annotation.definitionFit: The dormouse spends much of its life asleep, hibernating for months.

entries.clue: Young Nicklaus earned this in leading positions (5,6)

definitions.text: Young Nicklaus earned this in leading positions

indicators.note: take the letters that lead each word

blocks.note: first letters of earned and this

annotation.surface: Jack Nicklaus as a young man won the top prize while leading the field.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: Nicklaus won his first Masters green jacket at 23, from the front.
annotation.definitionFit: The green jacket is awarded to the winner of the Masters golf tournament, which Nicklaus won six times.

entries.clue: One cycling with new type of light (4)

indicators.note: cycling moves the first letter round to the back

blocks.note: ONE with its O moved to the end

annotation.surface: A cyclist fits a new kind of bike lamp.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a bike-light scene, and 'cycling' fits it perfectly; in the wordplay it rotates a word rather than pedals.
annotation.definitionFit: Neon lights are glowing gas-filled tubes.

entries.clue: Thousands in disgrace abroad took part in untidy melee (10)

indicators.note: 'in' puts the thousands inside the rearranged letters, so MM ends up in the middle of the word
abroad = astray, all over the place

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, doubled for the plural

annotation.surface: Crowds of people, shamed overseas, got involved in a brawl.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests football fans disgraced abroad; the thousands are just two Ms.
annotation.definitionFit: To scrimmage is to take part in a confused scuffle.

entries.clue: See 9
Lifted cloak covering item with 50% off in Institute of Clay (10)

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means read upwards
CLOAK wraps round the other letters
a 50% discount halves the price, and here it halves the word, so two of ITEM's four letters go

blocks.note: the outer word, before it is lifted

annotation.surface: An institute of clay studies keeps a cloak draped over a half-price item.
annotation.walkthrough: CLOAK read upwards is KAOLC, which holds IN, IT and I: KAOL-INITI-C.
annotation.definitionFit: Kaolinite is the main mineral of china clay, so kaolinitic means consisting of that clay.

entries.clue: Reassign Spooner’s part of leg dance? (8)

indicators.note: Rev Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: swap the N and R sounds: knee rumba becomes 'ree numba'

annotation.surface: A dance move is renamed after the part of the leg it uses.
annotation.walkthrough: The swap works in a non-rhotic accent, where 'rumba' and the end of 'renumber' sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: To renumber items is to assign them new numbers.

entries.clue: Lots upset after vicar renounces allegiance (7)

indicators.note: upset knocks the letters out of order
the rearranged letters come after the vicar

blocks.note: Rev, short for Reverend, a vicar's title

annotation.surface: Many parishioners, unhappy with the vicar, leave the church.
annotation.walkthrough: The parish drama hides that 'Lots' is the fodder and the vicar is just REV.
annotation.definitionFit: To revolt is to rise against, or renounce allegiance to, a ruler.

entries.clue: Letters written in to Independent about Oregon's food cooked in a clay oven (8)

definitions.text: food cooked in a clay oven

indicators.note: the letters go round Oregon

blocks.note: the word 'to' spelt out as its letters: T and O
OR is the US postal code for Oregon

annotation.surface: Someone writes to The Independent about a food from Oregon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Letters written in to' looks like readers writing to the paper; it means the word 'to' spelt as its letters. The italics on 'Independent' make it the paper, but here it is just I.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: tandoori names food cooked in a tandoor, the traditional Indian clay oven.

entries.clue: Father knocked back a quick drink with the regulars (7)

indicators.note: knocked back = turned back to front

blocks.note: a snort is a quick nip of spirits

annotation.surface: Dad downs a quick one at the pub alongside the locals.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' is drinking talk in the surface and a reversal in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Patrons are the regular customers of a pub or shop; spectators at the Masters golf are also called patrons.

entries.clue: Third character in Enid Blyton novel about international aristocracy (8)

indicators.note: take the third letter of Enid
novel = new, so the letters take a new form
the rest wraps round international

annotation.surface: A literary study looks at the upper classes in an Enid Blyton book.
annotation.walkthrough: Enid Blyton was a prolific British children's author; 'novel' looks like a book of hers but means new, so BLYTON is rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the nobility is the titled upper class, and aristocracy names the same class.

entries.clue: Well-mannered partner of Lady Moray? (7)

blocks.note: a moray is a kind of eel

annotation.surface: A polite gentleman escorts an aristocratic woman called Lady Moray.
annotation.walkthrough: Lady Moray reads as a Scottish title (Moray is a region in Scotland); split it and a gent partners a lady while the moray is just an eel.
annotation.definitionFit: Genteel means polite and refined in manner.

entries.clue: Knock about with niece playing card game (8)

indicators.note: 'about' as in turned about, facing the other way, so the knock is read backwards
the letters of niece play about

blocks.note: a tap is a light knock

annotation.surface: Someone passes the time knocking about with their niece over a game of cards.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knock about with' reads as spending idle time together; 'about' actually belongs to the knock, not the company.
annotation.definitionFit: Patience is the British name for solitaire, a one-player card game.

entries.clue: Farage is manifestly displaying prejudice against senior citizens (6)

indicators.note: the letters are on show inside the words

annotation.surface: A jibe that the politician Nigel Farage openly shows bias against the old.
annotation.walkthrough: Nigel Farage is a British right-wing politician; the political jab is the camouflage, and the answer runs across his name and the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Ageism is discrimination on grounds of age, especially against older people.

entries.clue: Judge ejected from parties with A-listers (6)

indicators.note: the judge is thrown out of the word

blocks.note: the verb: she parties = she celebrates
to rate is to judge, to assess; these four letters come out of the middle

annotation.surface: A judge is thrown out of a party full of famous people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Parties' looks like a plural noun but is the verb, celebrates; take RATE out and CELEBS is left.
annotation.definitionFit: A-listers are top celebrities, celebs for short.

entries.clue: Heartless official in a tight spot (6)

indicators.note: the middle letter is removed

blocks.note: a coroner investigates sudden deaths; its central letter, the O, is removed

annotation.surface: A callous bureaucrat finds himself in a difficult situation.
annotation.walkthrough: CORONER loses its heart to leave CORNER; Amen Corner at Augusta, the Masters stretch, links this to 2 down and the golf theme.
annotation.definitionFit: To be in a corner is to be in a difficult position with no way out.

entries.clue: Short expletive heard on EastEnders - he caught her with a chopper! (10)

indicators.note: short = missing its last letter
said in a Cockney accent, with the H sounds dropped

blocks.note: copped = caught; drop the aitches, as a Cockney would

annotation.surface: A soap-opera line: someone swears as a man attacks a woman with an axe.
annotation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a British TV soap set in Cockney East London, where 'he' and 'her' lose their H; 'chopper' is slang for both an axe and a helicopter.
annotation.definitionFit: Chopper is informal for helicopter, from the sound of its rotor blades.

entries.clue: Turn left regularly in this game? (4)

indicators.note: 'regularly' means at regular intervals, so the letters are taken at a steady every-other spacing

annotation.surface: A game where the rules make you keep turning left.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turn left' reads as a direction; the golf theme runs through the puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: Golf is the game, and taking your turn in it follows a set order.

entries.clue: Italian race's banking arrangement (4)

blocks.note: the three-week Grand Tour cycle race held each May in Italy
a system of direct transfers between bank or post-office accounts

annotation.surface: A cycle race in Italy has a sponsor's banking deal.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive makes one phrase of it, as if the race owned the bank deal; it is two separate meanings side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: The Giro is the Italian cycling race, and giro is a bank-transfer system.

entries.clue: Initially statesmanlike, it's said Starmer is one on the slide (5)

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so only the word's opening letter is wanted
the name as spoken, not as spelt

blocks.note: Keir Starmer, the UK Prime Minister

annotation.surface: A statesmanlike Keir Starmer is said to be on a slippery slope in the polls.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On the slide' suggests falling popularity; it means on a ski slope.
annotation.definitionFit: A skier travels down snowy slopes.

entries.clue: Denounce senior manager's pay (8)

annotation.surface: Critics condemn a top executive's salary.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface tempts you to read 'Denounce' as the start of a sentence about fat-cat pay, and it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to execrate is to curse or condemn loudly, the same public condemnation as to denounce.
